_meta.why: The panel's limits have always said 'the same ocean reads differently on each' index while showing exactly one number. This file carries the others so the claim can be shown rather than asserted.
_meta.caution: These are NOT interchangeable and not even directly comparable. They differ in region, in baseline, and in AVERAGING WINDOW — a three-month seasonal mean cannot be set against a weekly value and read as disagreement. Each row states its own window. What the spread demonstrates is that 'how strong is this El Nino' has no single answer, not that any agency is wrong.

indices.label: ONI
indices.note: The index this page headlines. Absolute anomaly against a fixed 1991–2020 base.

indices.label: RONI
indices.region: Niño 3.4, relative to the tropical mean
indices.note: CPC's OFFICIAL headline index. Subtracts the tropical-mean warming trend, so it reads LOWER than ONI as the tropics warm. The page should arguably lead on this.

indices.label: Weekly Niño 3.4
indices.note: A single week, not a season. Runs hotter than the seasonal mean because it has not been averaged down.

indices.label: Relative Niño 3.4
indices.note: BoM uses a higher threshold (+0.8) than CPC (+0.5), so the same water clears a different bar. BoM calls the event 'firmly established' and forecasts values above anything since 1950.

indices.label: Troup SOI
indices.note: The ATMOSPHERE, not the ocean. Negative is El Niño-like. Confirms the ocean signal is coupled rather than SST-only.

spread.note: Ocean-temperature rows only; the SOI is a pressure index and is not part of the spread.
